Lesson 01

Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source

Why it matters

Retrieval-augmented generation finds passages first, then asks the model to answer from those passages.

Try it: Retrieval pipeline

Lesson
01 of 09
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Index clock
When documents change
Question clock
Every ask
Answer
Only from the short list

Use retrieval when the words that justify the answer live in a corpus: your notes, a policy set, a code repository, a product manual. Do not use it to decorate a question the model can already refuse, or to pretend you have searched the live web when you have not.

A useful answer has three parts

  1. The passages that were retrieved, with ids.
  2. An answer that uses those passages.
  3. A visible refusal when the passages do not contain the answer.

If you skip the third, the model will fill the gap and your citations will make the invention look official.

Practice

Name a corpus you actually have, even a folder of ten notes. Write two questions the corpus can answer and one it cannot. The third is a required test, not a trick.

Check

When should the system refuse?

Show the answer

When the retrieved passages do not contain the answer, even if the model could guess.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Mini retrieval

Six sample notes live in the page. Keyword overlap always runs. Preset questions also have a hand-set vector so you can see hybrid ranking. The answer is a template that quotes the winning chunk, or refuses. No model is called.

Lesson 02

Chunk documents so a citation can point at them

Why it matters

Split on structure. Keep a stable id. Do not hunt for a magic token count.

Try it: Vector index

Lesson
02 of 09
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Split on
Structure
Id
Stable
Keep
The heading

A chunk is the unit you retrieve and the unit you cite. If a chunk mixes three topics, the citation cannot tell the reader which one supported the sentence. If a chunk splits a procedure in half, the answer will miss a step.

  • Prefer boundaries you already have: headings, functions, list items, speaker turns.
  • Give every chunk a stable id that survives a re-index, or record the old-to-new map when you rechunk.
  • A little overlap can keep a sentence that crosses a boundary. Overlap is a copy. It costs index size.
  • Store the source title, the heading path, and a character or line span with the chunk.
  • Record the chunker version in the artifact. A retrieval change you cannot name is a retrieval change you cannot debug.

Start with a boring size that respects headings. Change it when the eval says the right fact is split or buried, not when a blog names a different number.

Practice

Take one real page and mark the chunk boundaries with a pencil. Write an id scheme, such as note-14#setup. Check that each chunk still makes sense alone.

Check

Why is there no universal best chunk size?

Show the answer

Because the right boundary is the structure of the document and the questions you ask, which you measure.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Lesson 03

Search with keywords and with embeddings

Why it matters

Embeddings find similar meaning. Keywords find the exact name. Hybrid search uses both.

Try it: Embedding space

Lesson
03 of 09
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Keywords
Exact strings
Vectors
Paraphrase
Do not mix
Two embedding models

An embedding model turns text into a vector so you can search by similarity. It is not the chat model. Pin the embedding model the same way you pin a chat model. If you change it, re-embed the corpus. Mixed vectors in one index are silent nonsense.

Keyword search, such as BM25, finds the rare exact string: an error code, a function name, a SKU. Embeddings miss those and find paraphrases. Hybrid retrieval runs both and merges the lists. That combination is the ordinary 2026 default, not an advanced trick.

QueryBetter first net
NullPointerException in CartServiceKeywords.
How do we handle a customer who wants a refund after 30 days?Embeddings, if the policy uses different words.
The policy section that mentions SKU 1842 and replacementsBoth. Hybrid.

Practice

Write one query that needs an exact string and one that is a paraphrase of a heading in your corpus. Note which search should find each.

Check

What do you re-embed when you change embedding models?

Show the answer

The whole corpus. Old vectors are not comparable to new ones.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Cosine similarity

Cosine is the dot product divided by the two lengths. These vectors are hand-set teaching numbers, not the output of an embedding model.

Vector A
Vector B

Embedding space, drawn in 2D

A picture of a toy space. Real embedding vectors have hundreds or thousands of dimensions. Click a point to mark its nearest neighbors by ordinary distance in this drawing.

Lesson 04

Rerank a short list before you prompt

Why it matters

Retrieve widely, then keep the few passages that actually answer.

Try it: Retrieval pipeline

Lesson
04 of 09
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Wide
The first retrieval
Narrow
The reranker
Prompt
Only the survivors

The first-stage search is tuned to recall: do not miss the right chunk. That list is too long and too noisy to paste into the prompt. A reranker, or a simple second score, reads the question and each candidate and keeps the best few.

Reranking is cheaper than stuffing thirty chunks into a frontier model, and it reduces the chance that a vaguely related paragraph outshouts the real one. It does not create a passage you failed to retrieve. If the right chunk was never in the candidate list, fix the first stage.

  • Candidate count is a recorded parameter. Start around 20 and keep 4 to 6.
  • The reranker is its own model id. Pin it.
  • If you have no reranker, a documented rule such as 'keyword hit outranks a weak vector hit on error codes' is still a second stage. Write it down.

Practice

For one question, list five candidate chunks you would expect, in the order a person would keep them. Circle the ones you would actually paste into the prompt.

Check

What failure can a reranker not repair?

Show the answer

A first stage that never retrieved the right chunk.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Retrieval5 of 9Core11 min

Lesson 05

Cite a passage a person can open

Why it matters

A citation is an id and a span, not a confident tone.

Try it: Retrieval pipeline

Lesson
05 of 09
Time
11 min
Level
Core
Citation
Id plus span
Must be
Openable
Not a citation
A confident tone

Require the answer to name the chunk ids it used. Render those ids as labels a person can click or open. If the model cites an id that was not in the retrieved set, drop the sentence or fail the answer. That check is code.

A citation format that helps

Refunds after 30 days are refused unless a manager approves. [policy-4#refunds]

policy-4#refunds — Handbook / Refunds / After 30 days — lines 40–58

Quote the supporting span when the decision is risky. A paraphrase with a footnote is easier to drift. The quote is the artifact. The paraphrase is the interface.

The model will invent ids

That is normal. The repair is the membership check, plus an eval row where a fake id is the wrong answer.

Practice

Write the citation line you want for one chunk in your corpus: id, title path, and span. Then write the rule your code will apply if the model cites anything else.

Check

What makes a citation checkable?

Show the answer

It names an id you retrieved and a place in that source a person can find.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Retrieval6 of 9Practice10 min

Lesson 06

Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt

Why it matters

Wrong chunk, stale chunk, lost middle, and a corpus that never contained the fact.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
06 of 09
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Four failures
Wrong, stale, middle, missing
Before
Prompt adjectives
Missing fact
Say so

When a grounded assistant is wrong, look at the pipeline in order. Prompt edits are last.

SymptomLook here first
The right fact is in the corpus and not in the promptChunking or retrieval. The answer never had a chance.
The right chunk was retrieved and the answer ignored itPrompt, context order, or too many distracting chunks.
The answer cites a paragraph you have since rewrittenFreshness. The index is older than the source. Record the index time.
The answer invents a policy you do not haveMissing refusal. The corpus does not contain it, and the prompt allowed a guess.
A buried sentence in a long paste is ignoredLost-in-the-middle. Retrieve and place the passage. Do not paste the book.

Agentic retrieval — letting a model search again and again — comes after this table is mostly green. A loop on a broken index spends tokens to miss the same chunk.

Practice

Write one fixture row for each row of the table, using your corpus or a synthetic page. You only need the question, the expected chunk id or the expected refusal, and the failure name.

Check

A fluent answer cites nothing and sounds right. Where do you look first?

Show the answer

At whether any retrieved chunk contained the claim. If none did, the failure is retrieval or refusal, not prose style.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.
lessons.05-07:
Retrieval7 of 9Practice11 min

Lesson 07

Measure retrieval before you measure the answer

Why it matters

Recall on the right chunk is a different number from whether the paragraph was helpful.

Try it: Eval gate

Lesson
07 of 09
Time
11 min
Level
Practice
First score
Retrieval recall
Then
The written answer
Label
must_include ids

Build a small labeled set: question, and the chunk ids that must appear. Run retrieval alone. Report how often the right id is in the top 5, and how often it is the one you would have pasted. That is the retrieval metric.

Only then score the written answer. If retrieval recall is poor, an answer score mostly measures luck and invention. Fix the index, the embedding model, the keywords, or the chunks. Then rescore.

question: When is a manager required for a refund?
must_include: [policy-4#refunds]
top5_hit: true
pasted_hit: true

Freshness

Add the source's updated time and the index time to the artifact. A perfect score on last month's export is not a score on today's policy.

Practice

Create five labeled questions in the format above. If you cannot name a must_include id, you do not have a retrieval test yet. You have a vibe.

Check

Why score retrieval separately from the answer?

Show the answer

Because a wrong passage cannot be saved by the writer, and a right passage can still be ignored. The two failures have different fixes.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

[cite:1] h l1 · why retrieve if the model already generates fluent answers? p fluency is not provenance, and weights do not update when a policy pdf changes. the paper calls out limited precise access to knowledge, missing provenance, and the difficulty of updating world knowledge, and it shows a non-parametric index you can replace. [cite:1] h l2 · how does a question become a cited answer, end to end? p ingest: chunk, embed with a pinned model, store vector plus ids. query: embed the question with that same model, take top-k under a metadata filter, pack the texts with their ids, ask a frozen model to answer only from them or abstain, then intersect cited ids with packed ids. [cite:2] [cite:4] h l2 · where does the 2020 paper differ on that path? p the paper fine-tunes bart-large and the query encoder, freezes the document encoder, and marginalizes documents with rag-sequence or rag-token. it does not call a frozen chat api and it does not use cosine on openai vectors. [cite:1] h l3 · the answer is wrong. how do i prove which stage failed? p look at the trace in order. was the gold chunk in the index? did the filter remove it? did top-k include it? did the pack include it? did the model cite it? did application code accept a citation that was not packed? the first “no” is the stage. a wrong answer with an empty retrieved set is abstention failure, not a bad cosine. [cite:1] h l3 · what single query tells me the index is innocent? p embed the gold chunk’s text and the question with the stored model id and compute cosine, or run the sql with the filter removed. if the gold chunk ranks first in sql and the bot still misses it, the bug is after retrieval: pack, prompt, or the string the bot actually embedded. [cite:4] h l4 · how does this differ across pgvector and a hosted vector service, and across model vendors? p the pipeline does not change: same embedding model on both sides, a filter, a pack, an abstention check. pgvector’s operators and hnsw operator classes are cited. as of 2026-10-14, pinecone’s database-limits overview separates rate, object, operation, and identifier limits by plan and says many can be raised. read that page for the plan you buy. filtering syntax for a hosted service is that service’s page. [cite:8] openai’s cosine recommendation is for their embeddings guide, not a law of every vendor. if another vendor’s model card demands inner product, follow the card. [cite:2] [cite:4] h l4 · how does retrieval sit on a webex or ucce assist desktop? p the phone system still owns the call. the retriever runs on the transcript so far, or on the agent’s question, and the pack must be allowed for that caller and that queue. screen-pop of a cited article is a ui action. transfer is still a route. this room does not name that gadget. the retrieval math does not become sip. h l5 · if i redesigned this pipeline, what would i change, and what stops me? p i would store the rendered pack and the scores as first-class records, refuse uncited claims in code rather than in a prompt, and re-embed automatically when the embedding model id changes. what stops a casual redesign is the token budget of the chat model, the license to send corpus text to the embedding vendor, and the cost of rebuilding the index. as of 2026-10-14, openai’s models page lists a 1.05m-token context window and a 128k max output for gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna. embedding prices as of 2026-10-14 are on the pricing page cited here. the license to send a given corpus is still the content owner’s contract. The citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date.</p></aside><p>Retrieval-augmented generation, in the system you will actually ship, is a pipeline: chunk a corpus, embed it with one model, search, pack a few passages into the prompt, and require the language model to answer from those passages or abstain. The 2020 paper that named RAG is a related but stricter thing: a seq2seq model and a dense index trained so the generator is marginalized over retrieved documents. This room keeps those two meanings apart and walks the production path from document to cited answer.</p><h3>01Executive summary</h3><ul><li>The paper (Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020) combines a parametric seq2seq model with a non-parametric dense index of Wikipedia. The generator is BART-large. The retriever is initialized from Dense Passage Retrieval, a bi-encoder. They marginalize retrieved documents either once per output sequence (RAG-Sequence) or per token (RAG-Token). [cite:1]</li><li>What teams mean by RAG in 2026 is usually retrieve-then-read: a frozen chat model, an embeddings API, a vector index, and a prompt that says to use the retrieved text and to abstain otherwise. OpenAI’s embeddings guide demonstrates that shape: embed, rank by cosine similarity, and answer from the supplied article or say you do not know. [cite:2]</li><li>Query vectors and document vectors must come from the same embedding model. OpenAI documents default widths of 1536 and 3072 for two third-generation models and a <code>dimensions</code> parameter to shorten them. The embeddings API reference caps each input at 8192 tokens. [cite:2] [cite:3]</li><li>pgvector stores vectors in Postgres. Cosine distance is the <code><=></code> operator. Cosine similarity is one minus that distance. An HNSW index for cosine uses <code>vector_cosine_ops</code>. Hybrid search, in that README, means using Postgres full-text search as well and combining ranks with reciprocal rank fusion or a cross-encoder. [cite:4]</li><li>A fluent answer with no retrieved id in the trace is not grounded. The index can be replaced when facts change — that is the paper’s point about non-parametric memory — but only if you re-embed with the same model and you stop serving stale chunks. [cite:1]</li></ul><aside class="callout note"><h3>Why it matters for the lab engineer</h3><p>The grounded-assistant interview is this room drawn on a whiteboard: corpus, chunk, embed, filter, pack, cite, abstain, eval. Contact-center agent assist is the same pipeline pointed at a knowledge article and a CRM note, with the extra rule that the article’s license and the caller’s identity decide what may be retrieved. If you conflate the 2020 training recipe with a LangChain tutorial, a senior interviewer will notice. This room gives you the vocabulary to keep them separate.</p></aside><h3>02Architecture</h3><p>Production path. Ingest is steps 1–4. Query is steps 5–7. Numbers match the walk-through.</p><p>Diagram: Documents, chunks, embed, index, query, pack, answer</p><ul><li>1–4 run when the corpus changes, not on every question.</li><li>5 must use the embedding model id stored with the index.</li><li>6 is a pack with ids, not a dump of the top fifty chunks.</li><li>7 either cites those ids or abstains. A third behavior — inventing — is a failure.</li></ul><h3>Mermaid source for a later redraw</h3><pre><code>flowchart TB
  subgraph ingest [Ingest]
    D[Documents] --> C[Chunks with ids]
    C --> E[Embed]
    E --> I[Index plus metadata]
  end
  Q[Question] --> EQ[Embed with the same model]
  EQ --> S[Top-k and filter]
  I --> S
  S --> P[Pack under a token budget]
  P --> L[Frozen chat model]
  L --> A[Cited answer or abstain]</code></pre><p>The paper’s diagram is different. There the retriever is a probabilistic component p(z|x), the generator is a seq2seq model conditioned on a latent document, and training marginalizes that latent with a top-k approximation. You do not need to reproduce that training loop to ship retrieve-then-read. You do need to know it exists so you do not cite “RAG” and describe the wrong system. [cite:1]</p><h3>03Deep dive</h3><p>T1 established that a language model scores next tokens from whatever ids are in the window. RAG, in production, is how a specific paragraph gets into that window on purpose, with an id you can show later. If the paragraph never arrives, the model is back to parametric memory: fluent, and free to be wrong. The 2020 paper uses those words. Parametric memory is the generator’s weights. Non-parametric memory is the dense index. They showed you can replace the index to update what the system knows. [cite:1]</p><p>The generation model and the embedding model are different ids. The retrieval lesson does not depend on which generation id a vendor’s sample happens to print. OpenAI’s text guide, retrieved 2026-10-14, says the Responses <code>output</code> array can contain tool calls, not only text, and its code samples print <code>model: "gpt-6-astra"</code>. That string is an example on the page that day. A tool result that carries a retrieved passage is untrusted input, the same way a packed chunk is. MCP revision 2025-11-25 adds Resources as a server feature for context and data. That does not move the filter into the model. The host still decides which passages are allowed for this caller before anything is packed. [cite:13] [cite:14]</p><h3>What the paper actually built</h3><p>Lewis and co-authors treat the retrieved document as a latent variable. RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document for every token of the output. RAG-Token may use a different document for each output token. In both cases they approximate the sum over documents by the top k from the retriever. For RAG-Sequence the sequence probability is a sum, over those documents, of retriever probability times the full sequence probability under the generator. For RAG-Token the next-token probability is itself a sum over documents, and the sequence probability is the product of those mixtures. When the target is a single class label, the two formulas coincide because the sequence has length one. [cite:1]</p><p>The retriever is DPR: a query encoder and a document encoder, both initialized from BERT base in their description, scoring documents by inner product. Finding the top documents is maximum inner-product search. They initialize from a DPR checkpoint trained to retrieve passages that contain answers to TriviaQA and Natural Questions. The generator is BART-large, which they describe as a pretrained seq2seq transformer with 400 million parameters. Input and retrieved text are concatenated. They fine-tune the query encoder and BART. They keep the document encoder and the index fixed, because rebuilding the index whenever the document encoder moves is expensive, and they report they did not need that step for strong results. [cite:1]</p><p>Those are historical design choices. BART-large’s 400 million parameters are not the size of a 2026 chat model. The Wikipedia index is not your help center. The paper’s reported gains on Natural Questions, WebQuestions, and CuratedTrec are 2020 results. Cite them as the paper’s claims, not as a promise about your corpus. It recommends cosine similarity and says the choice of distance typically does not matter much. It also says third-generation vectors can be shortened with <code>dimensions</code>. Their guide claims that a <code>text-embedding-3-large</code> vector shortened to 256 still outperformed an unshortened <code>text-embedding-ada-002</code> vector of length 1536 on MTEB. That is their benchmark claim, tied to that write-up. It is not a promise about your help center. [cite:2]</p><p>The embeddings API reference lists models including <code>text-embedding-ada-002</code>, <code>text-embedding-3-small</code>, and <code>text-embedding-3-large</code>. [cite:3] A chunker that emits a chunk over 8192 tokens cannot embed it on that API without splitting again. As of 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s models page lists a 1.05M-token context window and a 128K max output for gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna. [cite:6]</p><p>pgvector’s README defines the operators: <code><-></code> is L2 distance, <code><#></code> is negative inner product, <code><=></code> is cosine distance, <code><+></code> is L1. Cosine similarity is one minus cosine distance. An HNSW index that supports cosine ordering is created with <code>vector_cosine_ops</code>. The same README says to use full-text search alongside vectors for hybrid search, and to combine results with reciprocal rank fusion or a cross-encoder. It does not, in that section, lock the fusion constant. The README does not lock a fusion constant, so there is no official default to copy. Pick one, write it down, and test recall. [cite:4]</p><p>Order by distance ascending if the operator is a distance. Ordering by <code><=></code> descending ranks the worst neighbors first. That single sort direction is a common reason a demo “retrieves” irrelevant text while the vectors are fine.</p><h3>A toy neighbor, so the metric is real</h3><p>These are not model outputs. They are two-dimensional vectors chosen so the arithmetic fits on a page. Query q = [0.85, 0.15]. Chunk A = [0.90, 0.10]. Chunk B = [0.20, 0.80]. Cosine is the dot product divided by the product of the Euclidean norms.</p><p>Norm of q is the square root of 0.85² + 0.15², about 0.863. Norm of A is about 0.906. Dot product is 0.85×0.90 + 0.15×0.10 = 0.780. Cosine is about 0.780 / (0.863 × 0.906) ≈ 0.997. Norm of B is about 0.825. Dot product is 0.85×0.20 + 0.15×0.80 = 0.290. Cosine is about 0.290 / (0.863 × 0.825) ≈ 0.407. A is the neighbor. In pgvector, cosine distance to A is about 1 − 0.997 = 0.003, and to B about 0.593. <code>ORDER BY embedding <=> q LIMIT 1</code> returns A. [cite:4]</p><p>Toy cosines. Not an embedding model. The gap is the whole lesson: the outage-shaped vector beats the billing-shaped vector.</p><p>A real embedding model does this in hundreds or thousands of dimensions, and the gap is often much smaller. The operators do not change. What changes is that you must measure recall on your questions instead of trusting a two-dimensional drawing. Neither the pgvector README nor the OpenAI embeddings guide states a universal chunk size. Overlap between chunks is a knob you justify with a recall test, not a folklore fraction.</p><h3>Packing and abstention</h3><p>The embeddings guide’s question-answering sketch puts an article in the prompt and tells the model to answer from it, and to say it does not know when the answer is not there. [cite:6] Spend the budget on the instruction, the question, and the chunks, in that order of protection: if you must cut, cut the lowest-ranked chunk, not the abstention rule. The 2020 paper means a specific probabilistic model that marginalizes a latent document. Say which one you mean. [cite:1]</p><h3>L1 · Why retrieve if the model already generates fluent answers?</h3><p>Fluency is not provenance, and weights do not update when a policy PDF changes. The paper calls out limited precise access to knowledge, missing provenance, and the difficulty of updating world knowledge, and it shows a non-parametric index you can replace. [cite:1]</p><h3>L2 · How does a question become a cited answer, end to end?</h3><p>Ingest: chunk, embed with a pinned model, store vector plus ids. Query: embed the question with that same model, take top-k under a metadata filter, pack the texts with their ids, ask a frozen model to answer only from them or abstain, then intersect cited ids with packed ids. [cite:2] [cite:4]</p><h3>L2 · Where does the 2020 paper differ on that path?</h3><p>The paper fine-tunes BART-large and the query encoder, freezes the document encoder, and marginalizes documents with RAG-Sequence or RAG-Token. It does not call a frozen chat API and it does not use cosine on OpenAI vectors. [cite:1]</p><h3>L3 · The answer is wrong. How do I prove which stage failed?</h3><p>Look at the trace in order. Was the gold chunk in the index? Did the filter remove it? Did top-k include it? Did the pack include it? Did the model cite it? Did application code accept a citation that was not packed? The first “no” is the stage. A wrong answer with an empty retrieved set is abstention failure, not a bad cosine. [cite:1]</p><h3>L3 · What single query tells me the index is innocent?</h3><p>Embed the gold chunk’s text and the question with the stored model id and compute cosine, or run the SQL with the filter removed. If the gold chunk ranks first in SQL and the bot still misses it, the bug is after retrieval: pack, prompt, or the string the bot actually embedded. [cite:4]</p><h3>L4 · How does this differ across pgvector and a hosted vector service, and across model vendors?</h3><p>The pipeline does not change: same embedding model on both sides, a filter, a pack, an abstention check. pgvector’s operators and HNSW operator classes are cited. As of 2026-10-14, Pinecone’s database-limits overview separates rate, object, operation, and identifier limits by plan and says many can be raised. Read that page for the plan you buy. Filtering syntax for a hosted service is that service’s page. [cite:8] OpenAI’s cosine recommendation is for their embeddings guide, not a law of every vendor. If another vendor’s model card demands inner product, follow the card. [cite:2] [cite:4]</p><h3>L4 · How does retrieval sit on a Webex or UCCE assist desktop?</h3><p>The phone system still owns the call. The retriever runs on the transcript so far, or on the agent’s question, and the pack must be allowed for that caller and that queue. Screen-pop of a cited article is a UI action. Transfer is still a route. This room does not name that gadget. The retrieval math does not become SIP.</p><h3>L5 · If I redesigned this pipeline, what would I change, and what stops me?</h3><p>I would store the rendered pack and the scores as first-class records, refuse uncited claims in code rather than in a prompt, and re-embed automatically when the embedding model id changes. What stops a casual redesign is the token budget of the chat model, the license to send corpus text to the embedding vendor, and the cost of rebuilding the index. As of 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s models page lists a 1.05M-token context window and a 128K max output for gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna. Embedding prices as of 2026-10-14 are on the pricing page cited here. The license to send a given corpus is still the content owner’s contract. [cite:6] [cite:7] The paper already shows the expensive version of an index rebuild: they froze the document encoder to avoid it. [cite:1]</p><h3>L5 · What does a better chat model not fix?</h3><p>A missing filter, a mixed embedding space, or a stale row. A stronger generator is more convincing when it fills a gap. The abstain check has to sit in your process. [cite:2]</p><h3>Leaf · Why is cosine similarity one minus pgvector’s cosine operator?</h3><p>The README defines <code><=></code> as cosine distance and tells you to subtract it from 1 to get similarity. You sort the distance ascending to get the nearest neighbor. [cite:4]</p><h3>Leaf · What did RAG-Token change relative to RAG-Sequence?</h3><p>RAG-Token can assign a different latent document to each output token. RAG-Sequence uses one document for the whole sequence. They match when the output length is one. [cite:1]</p><h3>Leaf · When do I reach for hybrid search?</h3><p>When the question is a rare string — an error code, a SKU, a proper noun — and vector neighbors miss the gold chunk that full-text search would hit. The README names the combination and names RRF or a cross-encoder as the fuse. It does not give you a recall guarantee. [cite:4]</p><h3>09Lab</h3><ul><li>Goal: by hand, rank two toy chunks for one query with cosine, write the pgvector order-by that returns the winner, and draft a four-line pack that forces a citation or an abstention.</li><li>Prerequisites: T1-R01 lab completed on paper. Postgres is optional. An API key is optional. Do not ingest a real customer corpus. Any sample text you embed must be yours.</li><li>Step 1. Compute cosine for q=[0.85, 0.15], A=[0.90, 0.10], B=[0.20, 0.80]. Expected: A near 0.997, B near 0.407.</li><li>Step 2. Convert both to cosine distance with 1 − cosine. Expected: A near 0.003, B near 0.593. Write <code>ORDER BY embedding <=> q LIMIT 1</code> and say which row returns. [cite:4]</li><li>Step 3. Write a pack: an instruction to answer only from the labeled chunks or say “I don’t know,” chunk A with id <code>outage-14</code>, and the question about when the outage ended. Expected shape matches the embeddings guide’s “use the article / say you don’t know” pattern. [cite:2]</li><li>Step 4. Invent a bad model reply that cites <code>outage-99</code>. Apply the intersection check. Expected: reject.</li><li>Step 5. State whether your exercise was paper RAG or retrieve-then-read, in one sentence. Expected: retrieve-then-read. You did not marginalize a latent document or fine-tune BART.</li><li>Evidence: the arithmetic, the SQL fragment, the pack, and the rejected reply, on one page in your private notes.</li><li>Break-it: swap in a query vector from a “different model” by using [0.20, 0.80] as the query while pretending the index was built with the original embedding. Expected: B wins for the wrong reason. Recovery: refuse to query until model id and dimension match the index. [cite:2]</li><li>Optional: if you already run Postgres with pgvector, create a two-row table and the HNSW cosine index from the README and confirm the plan uses the index. Match the README at the commit you installed. This room does not copy a second syntax. [cite:4]</li><li>Reflection: where did you almost trust a fluent sentence that failed the id intersection?</li></ul><h3>10Quiz</h3><p>Multiple choice</p><h3>Q1. In the 2020 paper, non-parametric memory is:</h3><ol><li>The BART weights.</li><li>The dense vector index of documents.</li><li>The softmax temperature.</li><li>The chat template.</li></ol><h3>Reveal</h3><p>B. Parametric memory is the generator. [cite:1]</p><p>Multiple choice</p><h3>Q2. RAG-Sequence differs from RAG-Token because:</h3><ol><li>Only RAG-Token uses a retriever.</li><li>RAG-Sequence conditions the whole output on one retrieved document; RAG-Token may switch document per token.</li><li>RAG-Sequence is cosine search.</li><li>They are the same for every sequence length.</li></ol><h3>Reveal</h3><p>B. They coincide for a length-one target. [cite:1]</p><p>Multiple choice</p><h3>Q3. OpenAI’s embeddings guide tells you to rank documents by:</h3><ol><li>Edit distance on the raw strings.</li><li>Cosine similarity of embedding vectors.</li><li>BLEU against the query.</li><li>The chat model’s attention map.</li></ol><h3>Reveal</h3><p>B. [cite:2]</p><p>Multiple choice</p><h3>Q4. pgvector’s cosine distance operator is:</h3><ol><li><code><-></code></li><li><code><#></code></li><li><code><=></code></li><li><code><+></code></li></ol><h3>Reveal</h3><p>C. L2 is <code><-></code>, negative inner product is <code><#></code>, L1 is <code><+></code>. Similarity is 1 minus cosine distance. [cite:4]</p><p>Multiple choice</p><h3>Q5. Default vector length for text-embedding-3-large in the guide is:</h3><ol><li>256</li><li>1536</li><li>3072</li><li>8192</li></ol><h3>Reveal</h3><p>C. 1536 is the small model’s default. 8192 is the per-input token cap, not the width. 256 is an example of shortening. [cite:2] [cite:3]</p><p>Scenario</p><h3>Q6. You change only the query to text-embedding-3-large and leave last month’s small-model index in place. What happens?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>You search across incompatible vectors. Re-embed or revert. The guide’s two defaults are different widths, which makes the mismatch obvious, and even equal widths would not make different models comparable. [cite:2]</p><p>Scenario</p><h3>Q7. Top-1 is the gold chunk. The spoken answer states a different time and cites no id. Where is the bug?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>After retrieval: pack, instruction, or the application’s willingness to show an uncited claim. Do not rebuild the index first. The abstention pattern belongs in the prompt and the empty-citation check belongs in code. [cite:2]</p><p>Scenario</p><h3>Q8. A caller with no authentication receives another account’s balance sentence. What failed?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>The metadata filter, or the decision to retrieve at all. Ranking quality is irrelevant. Stop the path. This room does not name the CRM field. The control is not optional.</p><p>Draw it</p><h3>Q9. Draw ingest and query as two separate timelines and mark the only arrow that must use the same model id.</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Ingest: document → chunk → embed → index. Query: question → embed → search → pack → generate → check ids. The two embed steps share the model id and the dimension. The chat model id may differ. [cite:2]</p><p>Draw it</p><h3>Q10. Sketch RAG-Sequence versus RAG-Token for a three-token answer and two documents.</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Sequence: one document choice covers all three tokens. Token: each of the three positions may pick either document, and the probability mixes inside the product. [cite:1]</p><p>Short answer</p><h3>Q11. The paper froze which encoder, and why?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>The document encoder, and the index built from it, because updating it means rebuilding the index. They fine-tuned the query encoder and BART. [cite:1]</p><p>Short answer</p><h3>Q12. What does the embeddings guide say to do when the article does not contain the answer?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Say you do not know. The published sketch uses that instruction rather than asking the model to improvise. [cite:2]</p><p>Short answer</p><h3>Q13. Which column types does the pgvector README show for a 3-dimensional embedding?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>The examples use <code>vector(3)</code>. A later section says you may store the column as <code>vector</code> without a fixed width, and cast to <code>vector(3)</code> when you index or order. The width still has to match the model. [cite:4]</p><p>Scenario</p><h3>Q14. Recall of the gold chunk fell after you re-embedded with a new model id but kept the old index. What is the first repair?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Rebuild the index with the same embedding model that embeds the query. Mixing widths or models makes cosine a comparison of unlike spaces. Do not “fix” it by raising k until the old vectors happen to look close. [cite:2] [cite:4]</p><h3>11Audio slots</h3><p>The player loads a local silent placeholder. Studio replaces the takes.</p><p>Overview · 3–5 min</p><h3>Transcript prompt</h3><p>Explain retrieve-then-read to a senior engineer. In four sentences, contrast it with Lewis et al. 2020: BART-large, DPR, RAG-Sequence versus RAG-Token, frozen document encoder. Then state the same-model rule and the rule that cited ids must be a subset of packed ids. Do not invent chunk sizes or prices.</p><p>Deep dive · 8–12 min</p><h3>Transcript prompt</h3><p>Compute cosine for the toy vectors in the room, convert to cosine distance, and say the ORDER BY. Explain vector_cosine_ops in one sentence from the pgvector README. Then walk the failure where retrieval is correct and the answer is still wrong, ending on the application-level intersection check.</p><p>Oral drill · 2 min</p><h3>Transcript prompt</h3><p>Six rapid questions: define parametric versus non-parametric memory, define RAG-Token in one sentence, name the cosine distance operator, give the default width of text-embedding-3-large, say when hybrid search earns its place, and name one failure a bigger chat model will not fix.</p><h3>13Citations</h3><p>Ledger copy: cites/T3-R01.md. The map is ecosystem.html.</p><h3>Glossary</h3><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Term</th><th>Here</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Chunk</td><td>The unit you embed and the unit you cite.</td></tr><tr><td>Pack</td><td>The subset of chunks placed in one request, with ids.</td></tr><tr><td>Abstain</td><td>A deliberate non-answer when support is missing. <article class="lesson" id="05-p-t3r04" data-panel="lesson" data-school="05" data-title="Vector databases and hybrid search" data-search="05-p-t3r04 vector databases and hybrid search pgvector stores vectors in postgres and can index them with hnsw or ivfflat. bm25 is a lexical score, and elasticsearch documents it as the default similarity. reciprocal rank fusion combines ranked lists. this room keeps those three mechanisms in separate sentences so a design review cannot pretend one extension does all three. note verification source note: last-verified was left unmarked until a person checks the cited pages. the citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date. p pgvector stores vectors in postgres and can index them with hnsw or ivfflat. bm25 is a lexical score, and elasticsearch documents it as the default similarity. reciprocal rank fusion combines ranked lists. this room keeps those three mechanisms in separate sentences so a design review cannot pretend one extension does all three. h 01executive summary ul pgvector’s hnsw index is a multilayer graph. the readme says it has better query speed-recall than ivfflat, builds more slowly, and uses more memory. you can create it on an empty table. ivfflat divides vectors into lists and searches the lists closest to the query. it builds faster, uses less memory, and needs data before you create the index because it trains. [cite:1] filtering on those approximate indexes is applied after the index scan. since 0.8.0, iterative scans can keep looking. the readme’s examples set hnsw.ef_search, ivfflat.probes, and the iterative-scan modes. those are starting points, not a universal production setting. [cite:1] bm25 is elasticsearch’s default similarity. the 8.19 reference documents k1 default 1.2, b default 0.75, and discount_overlaps default true. pgvector does not implement bm25. postgres full-text search is a different feature, tsvector and ts_rank. do not write a sentence that says the extension “does hybrid bm25.” [cite:2] elasticsearch’s rrf retriever defaults rank_constant to 60, and the constant must be at least 1. a higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. the 8.19 guide’s rank_window_size defaults to 10 and must be at least the requested size. the page names combining a standard retriever with a knn or elser retriever as a primary use. the pgvector readme mentions reciprocal rank fusion as one way to fuse full-text and vectors and does not lock the constant. [cite:3] [cite:1] pinecone, weaviate, qdrant, milvus, and chroma are names of products. check that vendor’s limits page for the plan you pay for. pod size and payload caps vary by vendor, plan, and region, which is why a remembered number does not belong here. note why it matters for the lab engineer a contact-center bot that misses “refund policy” when the caller says “you owe me money back” is often a vector neighbor that never shared those words, or a lexical hit that never shared the embedding. hybrid search is how you stop choosing only one failure. it is not a license to mix embedding models, skip the filter, or quote a rank constant you did not write down. the caller hears one answer. you should be able to say which list it came from. h 02architecture p two lists, one fusion. vectors and lexical ranks stay separate until a documented combiner. p diagram: seven stages: chunks, embed, hnsw or ivfflat, lexical bm25 or tsvector, fuse with rrf, filter, pack ul 1–3 are the vector path. the index type is hnsw or ivfflat, not both on the same column unless you built two indexes on purpose. 4 is lexical. in elasticsearch that default is bm25. in postgres it is full-text search, not a pgvector operator. 5 fuses ranks. 6 is the metadata filter. 7 packs text for the model or abstains. p sequence: the application asks both indexes, then fuses, then packs. p diagram: app, postgres vector index, lexical index, fusion step, and the packer that labels untrusted text p the picture does not include a reranker. a cross-encoder over the fused list is the next room’s problem, and it can only reorder what fusion already returned. if both lists missed the gold chunk, fusion cannot invent it. h 03deep dive p t3-r01 already fixed the operators. cosine distance is `<=>`, l2 is `<->`, negative inner product is `<#>`, l1 is `<+>`. the query vector and the stored vectors come from the same embedding model. this room starts where that room stopped: which index structure you build, what a lexical score is, and how two ranked lists become one. [cite:1] h hnsw in the readme p hnsw builds a multilayer graph. the readme’s claim against ivfflat is better speed-recall at query time, a slower build, and more memory. because there is no training step, you may create the index on an empty table and insert later. the create statement in the readme looks like `create index ... using hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops)`, and the same pattern exists for `vector_ip_ops`, `vector_cosine_ops`, and `vector_l1_ops`. bit vectors have `bit_hamming_ops` and `bit_jaccard_ops`. build parameters in the example are `m = 16` and `ef_construction = 64`. at query time the example is `set hnsw.ef_search = 100`, and `set local` works inside a transaction. the filtering section mentions a default `hnsw.ef_search` of 40: if a filter matches 10 percent of rows, only about 4 rows match on average. that sentence is an illustration of post-filtering, not a recommendation to leave the default untouched. [cite:1] p a notice you should expect on a large build says the hnsw graph no longer fits in `maintenance_work_mem` after 100000 tuples. that is the readme’s notice text. it is a memory fact about the build, not a statement that 100000 is the largest legal index. raise the memory setting if you intend to build past it, and still measure recall on your questions. do not treat the notice as a capacity plan for a contact center. h ivfflat in the readme p ivfflat splits vectors into lists and searches the lists closest to the query. the readme says the build is faster and the index uses less memory than hnsw, with lower query performance. you need rows first. the index trains on them. starting points printed in the readme: set `lists` to rows divided by 1000 for up to a million rows, and to the square root of the row count above a million rows. start `probes` at the square root of `lists`. the example uses `lists = 100` and `set ivfflat.probes = 10`. if probes equals the number of lists, the search is exact nearest neighbor and the planner may ignore the index. those are starting points. a production contact-center index is whatever recall you measured, not the example’s 100. [cite:1] table hnsw ivfflat ['structure', 'multilayer graph', 'lists of vectors'] ['empty table', 'allowed. no training step.', 'not the path. load data, then index.'] ['build versus query', 'slower build, more memory, better query speed-recall in the readme’s comparison', 'faster build, less memory, lower query performance in that comparison'] ['query knob', 'hnsw.ef_search. example 100. filtering text mentions default 40.', 'ivfflat.probes. start near sqrt(lists). example 10.'] ['exact mode', 'not described as “probes = lists”', 'probes = lists is exact, and the planner may skip the index'] note the filter happens after the approximate scan the readme says filtering on approximate indexes is applied after the index scan. if you ask for the nearest refund article inside one product line, the graph may return neighbors from other products and the filter may then discard them, leaving you with too few rows. iterative scans, since version 0.8.0, exist for that case. `hnsw.iterative_scan` can be `strict_order` or `relaxed_order`. ivfflat’s iterative scan in the readme is `relaxed_order`. they stop at `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` or `ivfflat.max_probes`. the example max scan tuples is 20000. a partial index, `where (category_id = 123)`, is the other tool when the predicate is stable. [cite:1] h bm25 is not a pgvector operator p elasticsearch documents bm25 as the default similarity. k1 defaults to 1.2 and controls term-frequency saturation. b defaults to 0.75 and controls length normalization. discount_overlaps defaults to true. you can cite those three defaults from the 8.19 index-modules page. you cannot cite them as pgvector settings, because they are not in the pgvector readme. [cite:2] p postgres can rank text with `tsvector` and `ts_rank`. that is full-text search in the database you already use for vectors. it is a reasonable lexical list to fuse with `<=>`. it is not bm25 unless you have installed something that implements bm25 and you have read that project’s docs. this room did not fetch a postgres bm25 extension. if a teammate says “pgvector bm25,” correct the noun. the extension contributes the vector type and the vector indexes. the lexical score comes from elsewhere. [cite:1] table mechanism where it lives default this room will quote what not to say ['cosine hnsw', 'pgvector', 'vector_cosine_ops. build example m=16, ef_construction=64.', '“this index understands synonyms.” it understands distances.'] ['bm25', 'elasticsearch similarity', 'k1=1.2, b=0.75, discount_overlaps true, as of the 8.19 page.', '“pgvector’s bm25.”'] ['tsvector', 'postgres full-text', 'no k1 was fetched from a postgres manual in this pass. do not invent one.', '“this is elasticsearch.”'] ['rrf', 'elasticsearch retriever, or your own sql', 'rank_constant 60 on the elastic page. 8.19 rank_window_size default 10.', 'a constant the pgvector readme locked. it did not.'] table query knob index readme example ['hnsw.ef_search', 'hnsw', '100 in the query example. filtering text mentions 40 as the default.'] ['hnsw.iterative_scan', 'hnsw, since 0.8.0', 'strict_order or relaxed_order. max_scan_tuples example 20000.'] ['ivfflat.probes', 'ivfflat', '10 in the example. start near the square root of lists.'] ['ivfflat.iterative_scan', 'ivfflat, since 0.8.0', 'relaxed_order in the readme.'] h reciprocal rank fusion p elasticsearch’s rrf retriever combines two or more child retrievers. the 8.19 guide says rank_constant defaults to 60 and must be greater than or equal to 1. a higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. rank_window_size defaults to 10 in that guide and must be at least 1 and at least the requested size. the primary use case named on the page is to combine bm25, via a standard retriever, with a knn retriever or an elser retriever. later elastic docs exist. this room pins the 8.19 page it fetched on 2026-10-14 and also points at the current rest page so you can see if the window default moved. if the two pages disagree when you re-fetch, the disagreement is the fact. do not average them. [cite:3] [cite:4] p the pgvector readme’s hybrid sentence is shorter. it says you can combine full-text search with vectors using reciprocal rank fusion or a cross-encoder. it does not print 60. if you implement fusion in sql, write the constant in the query or the config, and test recall. copying elastic’s 60 into postgres is a choice you document, not a default postgres shipped. a cross-encoder is a second model that reads a short list. it is not rrf. rrf never opens the text. it only trusts the ranks the two lists already produced. note write the constant down a recall change after “we turned on hybrid” is unreadable if nobody recorded rank_constant, the lexical analyzer, the embedding model id, and ef_search or probes. the incident review will relitigate folklore. the record is four numbers and two model strings. h what this room will not invent p hosted vector databases differ in tenancy, filtering, and payload limits. pass 3 already failed to fetch several of those child pages cleanly. this pass does not fill the gap from memory. if you need a pinecone pod size, a qdrant payload cap, or a weaviate class limit, open that vendor’s page and cite it, then drop any mark. until that fetch, the comparison you are allowed to teach is the one above: pgvector’s two index types, elasticsearch’s bm25 defaults, and elasticsearch’s rrf defaults. chroma and milvus can sit in the ecosystem table as names. they do not sit in the limits table as numbers. p same-model discipline survives hybrid search. a lexical hit does not repair a query vector from text-embedding-3-large scored against a column of text-embedding-3-small. openai’s guide, fetched 2026-10-14, defaults those widths at 1536 and 3072 and recommends cosine. fusion will happily blend a nonsense vector ranking with a sensible bm25 ranking and still look “hybrid.” check the model id before you celebrate the fused list. [cite:5] p owasp llm08 is the reminder that embeddings are an attack surface: poisoned documents, cross-tenant neighbors, and vectors that smuggle instructions. a metadata filter after the scan is not a complete tenant boundary if the approximate scan already mixed customers and the iterative scan then worked hard to find more of the wrong tenant. partial indexes or a hard predicate the planner must respect belong in the design, and the security review belongs in t8. llm01 still applies to whatever text you pack. hybrid retrieval does not fully mitigate prompt injection. [cite:6] h four queries, one index p query a is the exact title “refund policy.” bm25, or a tsvector of the title, should surface the page whose heading is those words. a pure vector search might prefer a paragraph that talks around refunds without using the heading. if you only ship vectors, you will file a bug against the embedding model for a lexical miss. hybrid exists so the heading can win on rank even when the vector list preferred a paraphrase. p query b is “you took my money twice,” with no shared keywords. the lexical list may return nothing useful. the vector list may return the double-charge article if the embedding space put those phrases near each other. hybrid exists so a paraphrase is not punished for failing bm25. if the vector list is empty because the column was embedded with a different model, fusion will not save you. rebuild, as t3-r01 already said. p query c is “refund policy” plus a filter `product = voice` on a table that is mostly chat articles. hnsw returns approximate neighbors, then the filter discards them. you see three rows and blame recall. the readme’s post-filter warning is this incident. iterative scan or a partial index is the change. raising temperature on the language model is not. [cite:1] p query d is a tie: both lists return the gold article at different ranks, and a stale article ranks high on bm25 because the old heading still matches. rrf will blend the ranks. it will not know the document hash changed on tuesday. freshness is a filter or a sort on metadata you stored, not a property of k1. record the hash at index time. t5 grades whether the packed id is the current id. p across the four queries the lesson is which list failed. log both ranks and the fused rank. a single “score” that already mixed them cannot be debugged at 2 a.m. elasticsearch can return the child retrievers’ hits if you ask it to. your sql can return them because you wrote the query. either way, store them on the trace next to `gen_ai.operation.name` when you mean retrieval. the opentelemetry genai conventions this lab pins are commit 4e8a281. [cite:7] h how to talk about scale without inventing a vendor p scale, in this room, means the index still returns the gold chunk when the table is no longer a demo. the readme already tells you the shape of that problem. hnsw’s graph wants memory, and the notice at 100000 tuples is the build telling you maintenance_work_mem is the first cliff, not the last. ivfflat’s list count is a function of row count, so a table that grows from a hundred thousand rows to two million is not the same lists formula: below a million the readme says rows/1000, above a million it says the square root. recompute when you cross that line. leaving lists at the example value of 100 because it was in the snippet is how a large table gets a toy index. [cite:1] p query-time scale is ef_search or probes, and it is a recall-versus-latency knob you measure. the readme does not publish a millisecond budget. a contact center that needs the first token inside a voice budget still measures that budget in t7. this room’s contribution is to refuse a number you did not time, and to put the index knob in the same trace as the model call so a slow pack is not blamed on the sampler. if probes is high enough that ivfflat becomes exact, you may have purchased a sequential scan. explain is the tool. a dashboard that only shows “vector p95” without the plan will call that scan a victory because the answers got more accurate and hide that the index was not used. p hybrid scale has a second axis: the lexical window. elasticsearch’s 8.19 rrf page defaults rank_window_size to 10. ten documents is a small committee. a filter that already threw away most of a large corpus can make those ten the wrong ten. raise the window on purpose, record it, and accept the cost. do not raise it because a blog said 100, and do not leave it at 10 because the default felt official, if your recall set says the gold article was ranked 11th on one of the child lists. the child list’s rank is the evidence. the default is the starting point. [cite:3] p there is a third axis people skip because it is not an index parameter. ingest rate. openai’s rate-limits guide, fetched 2026-10-14, lists file ingest at 300 requests per minute per vector store id for that product’s vector stores. that number is not a pgvector setting and not an elasticsearch bulk-thread count. it is a reminder that “scale” on a hosted embedding api is a quota on the limits screen, while scale on your own hnsw build is memory and time. quote the 300 only when you are talking about that openai ingest path. [cite:9] p tenant scale is the axis that becomes an incident. a single hnsw graph over every customer, with a product filter applied after the scan, will degrade exactly as the readme’s 10-percent illustration predicts, and it will degrade worse when the tenant is one percent of the table. iterative scan spends more work to fill the limit. a partial index per tenant spends disk to avoid the mix. neither choice is free. the wrong choice is the one nobody wrote down, followed by a pack that contains another customer’s refund article. that defect is not a tuning anecdote. it is the reason llm08 is on the owasp list this lab already fetched. [cite:6] p when you present this to a design review, draw two boxes and a fuse, and put the numbers you will actually set under the boxes: operator class, m or lists, ef_search or probes, lexical engine, k1 and b if the engine is elasticsearch, rank_constant, window, embedding model id, and the predicate. if a box says “pinecone, 100 pods” and you cannot open the page, delete the box. the review can survive a missing vendor. it cannot survive a fabricated cap. the same rule keeps this room shorter than a market survey and more usable than one. p a worked fusion, so the constant is not a slogan: three articles, ranks starting at 1. policy is lexical rank 1 and vector rank 5. paraphrase is lexical rank 8 and vector rank 1. stale heading is lexical rank 2 and vector rank 9. with rank_constant 60, a document’s fused score is the sum over lists of 1/(60+rank). policy scores 1/61 plus 1/65. paraphrase scores 1/68 plus 1/61. stale scores 1/62 plus 1/69. you do not need a calculator to see that policy and paraphrase both sit near two sixtieths, and the stale article is close behind because lexical rank 2 is almost as strong as rank 1 when the constant is 60. that closeness is the point of a large constant: it stops a single first-place finish from erasing the other list. if you wanted the first place to dominate, you would lower the constant, document the change, and re-run the recall set. elastic’s page says the higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. the arithmetic above is how that sentence feels on three rows. it is not a proof that 60 is correct for your corpus. [cite:3] p operators still matter on the vector side of that example. if you built the index with vector_l2_ops and you query with cosine distance, you are not testing fusion. you are testing a mismatch. the readme’s operator classes are part of the create statement, not a hint you may ignore at query time. cosine distance remains `<=>`, and similarity is one minus that distance. order by the distance ascending if you want the nearest neighbor. a fused rank that used a similarity sorted backwards will look like “hybrid is random.” it is the order by. t3-r01’s operator table is still the law under this room’s indexes. [cite:1] p bit vectors are the readme’s other family, and they are easy to skip if you only embed floats. hamming and jaccard operator classes exist for bit columns. they are not a substitute for cosine on a float embedding, and they are not bm25. if a future design quantizes vectors to bits, cite the operator you built and measure recall again. do not assume the float hnsw graph and the bit index rank the same neighbors. the readme listing both is the permission to build them. it is not a claim that they agree. [cite:1] p partial indexes deserve a last concrete picture. `where (category_id = 123)` builds a graph that only contains that category. a query for category 123 can use it. a query for category 999 cannot, and should not fall through into someone else’s graph because the application forgot the predicate. write the predicate in the application and in the index. post-filtering is the safety net for predicates you cannot carve into the index. it is a weak net when the predicate is very selective, which is why iterative scan exists. use the net. prefer the carve when the predicate is stable. say which one you shipped. [cite:1] h 04walk-through ol chunk and label. same as t3-r01. each row has a document id, a hash, a product predicate, and text. no universal chunk size is cited here. embed once. store the model id on the row. openai’s small and large defaults are 1536 and 3072. do not mix them. [cite:5] build one vector index. hnsw if you need the readme’s query trade and can pay the build. ivfflat if you have data, want the faster build, and will measure the recall you gave up. operator class matches the distance you will query. class="lesson-num">Lesson 09</span></div><h1>Vector databases and hybrid search</h1><p class="why-kicker">Why it matters</p><p class="lede">pgvector stores vectors in Postgres and can index them with
