The citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date.</p></aside><p>pgvector stores vectors in Postgres and can index them with HNSW or IVFFlat. BM25 is a lexical score, and Elasticsearch documents it as the default similarity. Reciprocal rank fusion combines ranked lists. This room keeps those three mechanisms in separate sentences so a design review cannot pretend one extension does all three.</p><h3>01Executive summary</h3><ul><li>pgvector’s HNSW index is a multilayer graph. The README says it has better query speed-recall than IVFFlat, builds more slowly, and uses more memory. You can create it on an empty table. IVFFlat divides vectors into lists and searches the lists closest to the query. It builds faster, uses less memory, and needs data before you create the index because it trains. [cite:1]</li><li>Filtering on those approximate indexes is applied after the index scan. Since 0.8.0, iterative scans can keep looking. The README’s examples set hnsw.ef_search, ivfflat.probes, and the iterative-scan modes. Those are starting points, not a universal production setting. [cite:1]</li><li>BM25 is Elasticsearch’s default similarity. The 8.19 reference documents k1 default 1.2, b default 0.75, and discount_overlaps default true. pgvector does not implement BM25. Postgres full-text search is a different feature, tsvector and ts_rank. Do not write a sentence that says the extension “does hybrid BM25.” [cite:2]</li><li>Elasticsearch’s RRF retriever defaults rank_constant to 60, and the constant must be at least 1. A higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. The 8.19 guide’s rank_window_size defaults to 10 and must be at least the requested size. The page names combining a standard retriever with a knn or ELSER retriever as a primary use. The pgvector README mentions reciprocal rank fusion as one way to fuse full-text and vectors and does not lock the constant. [cite:3] [cite:1]</li><li>Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and Chroma are names of products. Check that vendor’s limits page for the plan you pay for. Pod size and payload caps vary by vendor, plan, and region, which is why a remembered number does not belong here.</li></ul><aside class="callout note"><h3>Why it matters for the lab engineer</h3><p>A contact-center bot that misses “refund policy” when the caller says “you owe me money back” is often a vector neighbor that never shared those words, or a lexical hit that never shared the embedding. Hybrid search is how you stop choosing only one failure. It is not a license to mix embedding models, skip the filter, or quote a rank constant you did not write down. The caller hears one answer. You should be able to say which list it came from.</p></aside><h3>02Architecture</h3><p>Two lists, one fusion. Vectors and lexical ranks stay separate until a documented combiner.</p><p>Diagram: Seven stages: chunks, embed, HNSW or IVFFlat, lexical BM25 or tsvector, fuse with RRF, filter, pack</p><ul><li>1–3 are the vector path. The index type is HNSW or IVFFlat, not both on the same column unless you built two indexes on purpose.</li><li>4 is lexical. In Elasticsearch that default is BM25. In Postgres it is full-text search, not a pgvector operator.</li><li>5 fuses ranks. 6 is the metadata filter. 7 packs text for the model or abstains.</li></ul><p>Sequence: the application asks both indexes, then fuses, then packs.</p><p>Diagram: App, Postgres vector index, lexical index, fusion step, and the packer that labels untrusted text</p><p>The picture does not include a reranker. A cross-encoder over the fused list is the next room’s problem, and it can only reorder what fusion already returned. If both lists missed the gold chunk, fusion cannot invent it.</p><h3>03Deep dive</h3><p>T3-R01 already fixed the operators. Cosine distance is <code><=></code>, L2 is <code><-></code>, negative inner product is <code><#></code>, L1 is <code><+></code>. The query vector and the stored vectors come from the same embedding model. This room starts where that room stopped: which index structure you build, what a lexical score is, and how two ranked lists become one. [cite:1]</p><h3>HNSW in the README</h3><p>HNSW builds a multilayer graph. The README’s claim against IVFFlat is better speed-recall at query time, a slower build, and more memory. Because there is no training step, you may create the index on an empty table and insert later. The create statement in the README looks like <code>CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops)</code>, and the same pattern exists for <code>vector_ip_ops</code>, <code>vector_cosine_ops</code>, and <code>vector_l1_ops</code>. Bit vectors have <code>bit_hamming_ops</code> and <code>bit_jaccard_ops</code>. Build parameters in the example are <code>m = 16</code> and <code>ef_construction = 64</code>. At query time the example is <code>SET hnsw.ef_search = 100</code>, and <code>SET LOCAL</code> works inside a transaction. The filtering section mentions a default <code>hnsw.ef_search</code> of 40: if a filter matches 10 percent of rows, only about 4 rows match on average. That sentence is an illustration of post-filtering, not a recommendation to leave the default untouched. [cite:1]</p><p>A notice you should expect on a large build says the HNSW graph no longer fits in <code>maintenance_work_mem</code> after 100000 tuples. That is the README’s notice text. It is a memory fact about the build, not a statement that 100000 is the largest legal index. Raise the memory setting if you intend to build past it, and still measure recall on your questions. Do not treat the notice as a capacity plan for a contact center.</p><h3>IVFFlat in the README</h3><p>IVFFlat splits vectors into lists and searches the lists closest to the query. The README says the build is faster and the index uses less memory than HNSW, with lower query performance. You need rows first. The index trains on them. Starting points printed in the README: set <code>lists</code> to rows divided by 1000 for up to a million rows, and to the square root of the row count above a million rows. Start <code>probes</code> at the square root of <code>lists</code>. The example uses <code>lists = 100</code> and <code>SET ivfflat.probes = 10</code>. If probes equals the number of lists, the search is exact nearest neighbor and the planner may ignore the index. Those are starting points. A production contact-center index is whatever recall you measured, not the example’s 100. [cite:1]</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th></th><th>HNSW</th><th>IVFFlat</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Structure</td><td>Multilayer graph</td><td>Lists of vectors</td></tr><tr><td>Empty table</td><td>Allowed. No training step.</td><td>Not the path. Load data, then index.</td></tr><tr><td>Build versus query</td><td>Slower build, more memory, better query speed-recall in the README’s comparison</td><td>Faster build, less memory, lower query performance in that comparison</td></tr><tr><td>Query knob</td><td>hnsw.ef_search. Example 100. Filtering text mentions default 40.</td><td>ivfflat.probes. Start near sqrt(lists). Example 10.</td></tr><tr><td>Exact mode</td><td>Not described as “probes = lists”</td><td>probes = lists is exact, and the planner may skip the index</td></tr></tbody></table></div><aside class="callout note"><h3>The filter happens after the approximate scan</h3><p>The README says filtering on approximate indexes is applied after the index scan. If you ask for the nearest refund article inside one product line, the graph may return neighbors from other products and the filter may then discard them, leaving you with too few rows. Iterative scans, since version 0.8.0, exist for that case. <code>hnsw.iterative_scan</code> can be <code>strict_order</code> or <code>relaxed_order</code>. IVFFlat’s iterative scan in the README is <code>relaxed_order</code>. They stop at <code>hnsw.max_scan_tuples</code> or <code>ivfflat.max_probes</code>. The example max scan tuples is 20000. A partial index, <code>WHERE (category_id = 123)</code>, is the other tool when the predicate is stable. [cite:1]</p></aside><h3>BM25 is not a pgvector operator</h3><p>Elasticsearch documents BM25 as the default similarity. k1 defaults to 1.2 and controls term-frequency saturation. b defaults to 0.75 and controls length normalization. discount_overlaps defaults to true. You can cite those three defaults from the 8.19 index-modules page. You cannot cite them as pgvector settings, because they are not in the pgvector README. [cite:2]</p><p>Postgres can rank text with <code>tsvector</code> and <code>ts_rank</code>. That is full-text search in the database you already use for vectors. It is a reasonable lexical list to fuse with <code><=></code>. It is not BM25 unless you have installed something that implements BM25 and you have read that project’s docs. This room did not fetch a Postgres BM25 extension. If a teammate says “pgvector BM25,” correct the noun. The extension contributes the vector type and the vector indexes. The lexical score comes from elsewhere. [cite:1]</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Mechanism</th><th>Where it lives</th><th>Default this room will quote</th><th>What not to say</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Cosine HNSW</td><td>pgvector</td><td>vector_cosine_ops. Build example m=16, ef_construction=64.</td><td>“This index understands synonyms.” It understands distances.</td></tr><tr><td>BM25</td><td>Elasticsearch similarity</td><td>k1=1.2, b=0.75, discount_overlaps true, as of the 8.19 page.</td><td>“pgvector’s BM25.”</td></tr><tr><td>tsvector</td><td>Postgres full-text</td><td>No k1 was fetched from a Postgres manual in this pass. Do not invent one.</td><td>“This is Elasticsearch.”</td></tr><tr><td>RRF</td><td>Elasticsearch retriever, or your own SQL</td><td>rank_constant 60 on the Elastic page. 8.19 rank_window_size default 10.</td><td>A constant the pgvector README locked. It did not.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Query knob</th><th>Index</th><th>README example</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>hnsw.ef_search</td><td>HNSW</td><td>100 in the query example. Filtering text mentions 40 as the default.</td></tr><tr><td>hnsw.iterative_scan</td><td>HNSW, since 0.8.0</td><td>strict_order or relaxed_order. max_scan_tuples example 20000.</td></tr><tr><td>ivfflat.probes</td><td>IVFFlat</td><td>10 in the example. Start near the square root of lists.</td></tr><tr><td>ivfflat.iterative_scan</td><td>IVFFlat, since 0.8.0</td><td>relaxed_order in the README.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><h3>Reciprocal rank fusion</h3><p>Elasticsearch’s RRF retriever combines two or more child retrievers. The 8.19 guide says rank_constant defaults to 60 and must be greater than or equal to 1. A higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. rank_window_size defaults to 10 in that guide and must be at least 1 and at least the requested size. The primary use case named on the page is to combine BM25, via a standard retriever, with a knn retriever or an ELSER retriever. Later Elastic docs exist. This room pins the 8.19 page it fetched on 2026-10-14 and also points at the current REST page so you can see if the window default moved. If the two pages disagree when you re-fetch, the disagreement is the fact. Do not average them. [cite:3] [cite:4]</p><p>The pgvector README’s hybrid sentence is shorter. It says you can combine full-text search with vectors using reciprocal rank fusion or a cross-encoder. It does not print 60. If you implement fusion in SQL, write the constant in the query or the config, and test recall. Copying Elastic’s 60 into Postgres is a choice you document, not a default Postgres shipped. A cross-encoder is a second model that reads a short list. It is not RRF. RRF never opens the text. It only trusts the ranks the two lists already produced.</p><aside class="callout note"><h3>Write the constant down</h3><p>A recall change after “we turned on hybrid” is unreadable if nobody recorded rank_constant, the lexical analyzer, the embedding model id, and ef_search or probes. The incident review will relitigate folklore. The record is four numbers and two model strings.</p></aside><h3>What this room will not invent</h3><p>Hosted vector databases differ in tenancy, filtering, and payload limits. Pass 3 already failed to fetch several of those child pages cleanly. This pass does not fill the gap from memory. If you need a Pinecone pod size, a Qdrant payload cap, or a Weaviate class limit, open that vendor’s page and cite it, then drop any mark. Until that fetch, the comparison you are allowed to teach is the one above: pgvector’s two index types, Elasticsearch’s BM25 defaults, and Elasticsearch’s RRF defaults. Chroma and Milvus can sit in the ecosystem table as names. They do not sit in the limits table as numbers.</p><p>Same-model discipline survives hybrid search. A lexical hit does not repair a query vector from text-embedding-3-large scored against a column of text-embedding-3-small. OpenAI’s guide, fetched 2026-10-14, defaults those widths at 1536 and 3072 and recommends cosine. Fusion will happily blend a nonsense vector ranking with a sensible BM25 ranking and still look “hybrid.” Check the model id before you celebrate the fused list. [cite:5]</p><p>OWASP LLM08 is the reminder that embeddings are an attack surface: poisoned documents, cross-tenant neighbors, and vectors that smuggle instructions. A metadata filter after the scan is not a complete tenant boundary if the approximate scan already mixed customers and the iterative scan then worked hard to find more of the wrong tenant. Partial indexes or a hard predicate the planner must respect belong in the design, and the security review belongs in T8. LLM01 still applies to whatever text you pack. Hybrid retrieval does not fully mitigate prompt injection. [cite:6]</p><h3>Four queries, one index</h3><p>Query A is the exact title “Refund policy.” BM25, or a tsvector of the title, should surface the page whose heading is those words. A pure vector search might prefer a paragraph that talks around refunds without using the heading. If you only ship vectors, you will file a bug against the embedding model for a lexical miss. Hybrid exists so the heading can win on rank even when the vector list preferred a paraphrase.</p><p>Query B is “you took my money twice,” with no shared keywords. The lexical list may return nothing useful. The vector list may return the double-charge article if the embedding space put those phrases near each other. Hybrid exists so a paraphrase is not punished for failing BM25. If the vector list is empty because the column was embedded with a different model, fusion will not save you. Rebuild, as T3-R01 already said.</p><p>Query C is “refund policy” plus a filter <code>product = voice</code> on a table that is mostly chat articles. HNSW returns approximate neighbors, then the filter discards them. You see three rows and blame recall. The README’s post-filter warning is this incident. Iterative scan or a partial index is the change. Raising temperature on the language model is not. [cite:1]</p><p>Query D is a tie: both lists return the gold article at different ranks, and a stale article ranks high on BM25 because the old heading still matches. RRF will blend the ranks. It will not know the document hash changed on Tuesday. Freshness is a filter or a sort on metadata you stored, not a property of k1. Record the hash at index time. T5 grades whether the packed id is the current id.</p><p>Across the four queries the lesson is which list failed. Log both ranks and the fused rank. A single “score” that already mixed them cannot be debugged at 2 a.m. Elasticsearch can return the child retrievers’ hits if you ask it to. Your SQL can return them because you wrote the query. Either way, store them on the trace next to <code>gen_ai.operation.name</code> when you mean retrieval. The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions this lab pins are commit 4e8a281. [cite:7]</p><h3>How to talk about scale without inventing a vendor</h3><p>Scale, in this room, means the index still returns the gold chunk when the table is no longer a demo. The README already tells you the shape of that problem. HNSW’s graph wants memory, and the notice at 100000 tuples is the build telling you maintenance_work_mem is the first cliff, not the last. IVFFlat’s list count is a function of row count, so a table that grows from a hundred thousand rows to two million is not the same lists formula: below a million the README says rows/1000, above a million it says the square root. Recompute when you cross that line. Leaving lists at the example value of 100 because it was in the snippet is how a large table gets a toy index. [cite:1]</p><p>Query-time scale is ef_search or probes, and it is a recall-versus-latency knob you measure. The README does not publish a millisecond budget. A contact center that needs the first token inside a voice budget still measures that budget in T7. This room’s contribution is to refuse a number you did not time, and to put the index knob in the same trace as the model call so a slow pack is not blamed on the sampler. If probes is high enough that IVFFlat becomes exact, you may have purchased a sequential scan. EXPLAIN is the tool. A dashboard that only shows “vector p95” without the plan will call that scan a victory because the answers got more accurate and hide that the index was not used.</p><p>Hybrid scale has a second axis: the lexical window. Elasticsearch’s 8.19 RRF page defaults rank_window_size to 10. Ten documents is a small committee. A filter that already threw away most of a large corpus can make those ten the wrong ten. Raise the window on purpose, record it, and accept the cost. Do not raise it because a blog said 100, and do not leave it at 10 because the default felt official, if your recall set says the gold article was ranked 11th on one of the child lists. The child list’s rank is the evidence. The default is the starting point. [cite:3]</p><p>There is a third axis people skip because it is not an index parameter. Ingest rate. OpenAI’s rate-limits guide, fetched 2026-10-14, lists file ingest at 300 requests per minute per vector store id for that product’s vector stores. That number is not a pgvector setting and not an Elasticsearch bulk-thread count. It is a reminder that “scale” on a hosted embedding API is a quota on the Limits screen, while scale on your own HNSW build is memory and time. Quote the 300 only when you are talking about that OpenAI ingest path. [cite:9]</p><p>Tenant scale is the axis that becomes an incident. A single HNSW graph over every customer, with a product filter applied after the scan, will degrade exactly as the README’s 10-percent illustration predicts, and it will degrade worse when the tenant is one percent of the table. Iterative scan spends more work to fill the limit. A partial index per tenant spends disk to avoid the mix. Neither choice is free. The wrong choice is the one nobody wrote down, followed by a pack that contains another customer’s refund article. That defect is not a tuning anecdote. It is the reason LLM08 is on the OWASP list this lab already fetched. [cite:6]</p><p>When you present this to a design review, draw two boxes and a fuse, and put the numbers you will actually set under the boxes: operator class, m or lists, ef_search or probes, lexical engine, k1 and b if the engine is Elasticsearch, rank_constant, window, embedding model id, and the predicate. If a box says “Pinecone, 100 pods” and you cannot open the page, delete the box. The review can survive a missing vendor. It cannot survive a fabricated cap. The same rule keeps this room shorter than a market survey and more usable than one.</p><p>A worked fusion, so the constant is not a slogan: three articles, ranks starting at 1. Policy is lexical rank 1 and vector rank 5. Paraphrase is lexical rank 8 and vector rank 1. Stale heading is lexical rank 2 and vector rank 9. With rank_constant 60, a document’s fused score is the sum over lists of 1/(60+rank). Policy scores 1/61 plus 1/65. Paraphrase scores 1/68 plus 1/61. Stale scores 1/62 plus 1/69. You do not need a calculator to see that policy and paraphrase both sit near two sixtieths, and the stale article is close behind because lexical rank 2 is almost as strong as rank 1 when the constant is 60. That closeness is the point of a large constant: it stops a single first-place finish from erasing the other list. If you wanted the first place to dominate, you would lower the constant, document the change, and re-run the recall set. Elastic’s page says the higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. The arithmetic above is how that sentence feels on three rows. It is not a proof that 60 is correct for your corpus. [cite:3]</p><p>Operators still matter on the vector side of that example. If you built the index with vector_l2_ops and you query with cosine distance, you are not testing fusion. You are testing a mismatch. The README’s operator classes are part of the create statement, not a hint you may ignore at query time. Cosine distance remains <code><=></code>, and similarity is one minus that distance. Order by the distance ascending if you want the nearest neighbor. A fused rank that used a similarity sorted backwards will look like “hybrid is random.” It is the ORDER BY. T3-R01’s operator table is still the law under this room’s indexes. [cite:1]</p><p>Bit vectors are the README’s other family, and they are easy to skip if you only embed floats. Hamming and Jaccard operator classes exist for bit columns. They are not a substitute for cosine on a float embedding, and they are not BM25. If a future design quantizes vectors to bits, cite the operator you built and measure recall again. Do not assume the float HNSW graph and the bit index rank the same neighbors. The README listing both is the permission to build them. It is not a claim that they agree. [cite:1]</p><p>Partial indexes deserve a last concrete picture. <code>WHERE (category_id = 123)</code> builds a graph that only contains that category. A query for category 123 can use it. A query for category 999 cannot, and should not fall through into someone else’s graph because the application forgot the predicate. Write the predicate in the application and in the index. Post-filtering is the safety net for predicates you cannot carve into the index. It is a weak net when the predicate is very selective, which is why iterative scan exists. Use the net. Prefer the carve when the predicate is stable. Say which one you shipped. [cite:1]</p><h3>04Walk-through</h3><ol><li>Chunk and label. Same as T3-R01. Each row has a document id, a hash, a product predicate, and text. No universal chunk size is cited here.</li><li>Embed once. Store the model id on the row. OpenAI’s small and large defaults are 1536 and 3072. Do not mix them. [cite:5]</li><li>Build one vector index. HNSW if you need the README’s query trade and can pay the build. IVFFlat if you have data, want the faster build, and will measure the recall you gave up. Operator class matches the distance you will query. [cite:1]</li><li>Build the lexical side separately. Elasticsearch index with the default BM25 similarity, or a Postgres tsvector. Do not look for a BM25 operator inside pgvector.</li><li>Query both. Set ef_search or probes explicitly in the session so the number is in the log. Take a window large enough that fusion has something to blend. Elastic’s 8.19 default window is 10. That may be too small for your filter. It is a default, not a moral law. [cite:3]</li><li>Fuse, filter, pack. Record the constant. Apply the tenant predicate. If the gold id is absent, abstain or widen the window. Do not ask the model to “remember the policy.”</li></ol><h3>05Config path</h3><p>There is no Control Hub page for HNSW. The admin surface is the database migration and the Elasticsearch index settings. Which bot calls the index is the tenant’s routing, not an HNSW setting. Check the admin guide for the product you run. Menu names differ by product and by the version installed on that tenant.</p><ol><li>Pin the pgvector commit or release you install. The README on master is what this room fetched on 2026-10-14. A later release can move defaults. [cite:1]</li><li>Choose the operator class before the first insert you care about. Changing cosine to L2 later is a new index, not a SET command.</li><li>For HNSW, start from the README example m and ef_construction, then change them only with a recall test. For IVFFlat, compute lists from the README’s row rules, load data, then index.</li><li>Set the query-time GUC in the application session: ef_search or probes. Log it.</li><li>If you filter, decide iterative scan versus a partial index before launch. Write max_scan_tuples if you set it. The example 20000 is an example. [cite:1]</li><li>If the lexical engine is Elasticsearch, record k1, b, rank_constant, and rank_window_size. If you left defaults, write “default as of the 8.19 page” and the fetch date. [cite:2] [cite:3]</li><li>Store the embedding model id. Refuse a query whose id differs.</li></ol><h3>06Limits and numbers</h3><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Limit</th><th>Value</th><th>Source</th><th>Stable enough to ship on</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>HNSW build example</td><td>m = 16, ef_construction = 64</td><td>[cite:1]</td><td>Yes as the README example. Caps vary by vendor, plan, and region. The names in this room are not caps.</td><td></td></tr></tbody></table></div><h3>08Self-question ladder</h3><p>Answer out loud. A leaf ends in a citation or a TODO-verify.</p><h3>L0 · What does pgvector contribute to hybrid search?</h3><p>The vector type and the approximate indexes, HNSW or IVFFlat, plus the distance operators. It does not contribute BM25. [cite:1]</p><h3>L1 · When can you build HNSW on an empty table?</h3><p>When you accept the README’s statement that HNSW has no training step. IVFFlat is the index that wants rows first. [cite:1]</p><h3>L1 · What does the README say HNSW trades against IVFFlat?</h3><p>Better query speed-recall, a slower build, and more memory. Those are the README’s comparisons, not your benchmark until you run one. [cite:1]</p><h3>L2 · Why does a selective filter return too few HNSW hits?</h3><p>Filtering is applied after the approximate index scan. With the default ef_search of 40 mentioned in that section, a filter that matches 10 percent of rows leaves about four hits on average. Iterative scan or a partial index is the documented response. [cite:1]</p><h3>L2 · What is probes equal to lists?</h3><p>Exact nearest neighbor for IVFFlat, and the planner may not use the index. [cite:1]</p><h3>L3 · Quote Elasticsearch BM25 defaults.</h3><p>k1 is 1.2, b is 0.75, discount_overlaps is true, on the 8.19 similarity page fetched 2026-10-14. [cite:2]</p><h3>L3 · Is ts_rank the same citation?</h3><p>No. Postgres full-text search was not given those k1 and b values in this room. Do not paste Elasticsearch defaults onto tsvector.</p><h3>L3 · What is rank_constant 60?</h3><p>The default on Elasticsearch’s RRF retriever. It must be at least 1. A higher constant gives lower-ranked documents more influence. The pgvector README does not lock this number. [cite:3] [cite:1]</p><h3>L4 · What did the 8.19 guide say about rank_window_size?</h3><p>It defaults to 10, and it must be at least 1 and at least the size you requested. Re-fetch the current REST page before you treat 10 as eternal. [cite:3] [cite:4]</p><h3>L4 · Why log both child ranks?</h3><p>Because a fused score hides which list failed. Query A in this room is a lexical win. Query B is a vector win. One number cannot tell them apart.</p><h3>L5 · If you redesigned the index, what would you change, and what stops you?</h3><p>I would partial-index by tenant and product before I raised ef_search, and I would record rank_constant in the same migration as the embedding model id. What stops a looser design is LLM08 and a pack that contains another customer’s article. Check the vendor’s limits page for the plan you pay for. Caps vary by vendor, plan, and region. [cite:6]</p><h3>Leaf · Where does a cross-encoder sit?</h3><p>After the fused list, on a short candidate set. It cannot recover a chunk both lists dropped. The README names it as an alternative to RRF, not as a synonym. [cite:1]</p><h3>Leaf · What embedding widths are you not allowed to mix?</h3><p>text-embedding-3-small defaults to 1536 and text-embedding-3-large to 3072 in OpenAI’s guide. Cosine is the recommended similarity. A hybrid lexical list does not excuse a mixed column. [cite:5]</p><h3>Leaf · Which pgvector release introduced iterative scans?</h3><p>0.8.0, as the README states. Modes named there include strict_order and relaxed_order for HNSW, and relaxed_order for IVFFlat. [cite:1]</p><h3>09Lab</h3><p>No database server is required. Paper or a local scratch query if you already have Postgres. Do not point this lab at a production cluster.</p><ol><li>Prerequisite: you can name <code><=></code> versus <code><-></code> from T3-R01.</li><li>Write two CREATE INDEX sketches, one HNSW and one IVFFlat, with the operator class you mean. Include m and lists only as README examples, labeled as examples. [cite:1]</li><li>Write the SET commands for ef_search and probes. State which index each belongs to.</li><li>On a napkin, rank three fake rows by “lexical” and by “vector,” then fuse with rank_constant 60 using 1/(constant+rank). Say which row moved. This is Elastic’s default constant used as arithmetic, not a claim that your cluster is Elasticsearch. [cite:3]</li><li>Mark one column “do not cite” for Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, and Chroma numeric limits.</li><li>Stop. Do not create an index on a shared production table from this page.</li></ol><h3>10Quiz</h3><p>Recall</p><h3>Q1. HNSW versus IVFFlat, as the README compares them:</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>HNSW has better query speed-recall, a slower build, and more memory. IVFFlat builds faster, uses less memory, and needs data before the index. [cite:1]</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q2. You want an index before the first insert. Which README path allows an empty table?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>HNSW. IVFFlat trains on existing rows. [cite:1]</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q3. A product filter matches 10 percent of rows and you only get a handful of neighbors.</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Approximate indexes filter after the scan. The README’s ef_search 40 illustration predicts about four matches. Use iterative scan or a partial index. [cite:1]</p><p>Recall</p><h3>Q4. Iterative scans arrived in which pgvector version, per the README?</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>0.8.0. [cite:1]</p><p>Recall</p><h3>Q5. Elasticsearch BM25 defaults on the 8.19 page:</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75, discount_overlaps true. [cite:2]</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q6. A migration comment says “enable pgvector BM25.”</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Strike it. BM25 defaults cited here are Elasticsearch’s. pgvector contributes vectors. Postgres FTS is tsvector, and this room does not claim that is BM25. [cite:2]</p><p>Recall</p><h3>Q7. RRF rank_constant default:</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>60, and it must be at least 1. Higher values give lower ranks more influence. [cite:3]</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q8. The pgvector README locks rank_constant at 60.</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>False. It mentions reciprocal rank fusion and does not lock the constant. 60 is the Elasticsearch retriever default. [cite:1] [cite:3]</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q9. IVFFlat with probes equal to lists:</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Exact nearest neighbor, and the planner may not use the index. [cite:1]</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q10. Hybrid search with two embedding model ids in one column.</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Still wrong. Lexical fusion does not repair mixed vector spaces. OpenAI’s guide separates 1536 and 3072 defaults. [cite:5]</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q11. A Pinecone pod size from memory in the limits table.</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Check that vendor’s limits page for the plan you pay for. Pod size varies by plan and region, so a number from memory is not a cite.</p><p>Apply</p><h3>Q12. Another tenant’s article survives into the pack.</h3><h3>Reveal</h3><p>Severity-1. Post-filtering an approximate scan is a known shape. Partial indexes and LLM08 apply. Do not raise temperature. [cite:6]</p><h3>11Audio</h3><p>Silence.
